Ion. Atoms or molecules that have gained or lost one or more electrons, acquiring a net electric charge. Atoms that lose electrons become positively charged cations, while atoms that gain electrons become negatively charged anions. Ions are fundamental to chemistry and biology, mediating ionic bonding, salt dissolution, electrical conductivity in solutions, and countless cellular processes like muscle contraction and nerve transmission.

An atom's charge state is determined by comparing its electron count—with a negative charge per electron of negative one—to its proton count, with a positive charge per proton of positive one. Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons. Cations are positively charged ions formed by electron loss. Metals readily form cations because valence electrons are loosely held. Sodium loses one electron to become sodium plus, and magnesium loses two to become magnesium two plus.

Anions are negatively charged ions formed by electron gain. Nonmetals readily form anions because they attract electrons strongly. Chlorine gains one electron to become chlorine minus, and oxygen gains two to become oxygen two minus. Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an atom. Lower ionization energy predicts easier cation formation, so metals have lower ionization energies than nonmetals.

Electron affinity is the energy change when an atom gains an electron. Elements with high electron affinity readily form anions, particularly the halogens and chalcogens. Ions differ dramatically from neutral atoms in their properties. Sodium metal is highly reactive and burns in air, but sodium cations in salt are inert. Chlorine gas is toxic, but chloride anions are essential electrolytes in the body.

Polyatomic ions contain multiple atoms covalently bonded together but with a net charge, such as sulfate, nitrate, and ammonium. In aqueous solution, ions dissociate and become solvated—surrounded by water molecules oriented by electrostatic attraction, with cations surrounded by the delta negative oxygen and anions by the delta positive hydrogen.

Ions are connected to atoms, which become ions through electron gain or loss, and to electrons themselves—the particles gained or lost in ionization that determine ionic charge. Ionic bonds form between cations and anions through electrostatic attraction, and electronegativity predicts which atoms preferentially lose electrons as metals or gain electrons as nonmetals. Electrolytes are solutions containing ions that conduct electricity, and salt is the archetypal ionic compound formed from cations and anions. Muscle contraction is driven by calcium and potassium ion flux.
